C005.subject: Free trade policies
C005.object: more persistent and severe income losses in import-competing sectors when those sectors are dominated by small and medium enterprises with limited access to credit
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade policies more persistent and severe income losses in import-competing sectors when those sectors are dominated by small and medium enterprises with limited access to credit]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal firm-level survey data from developing economies (e.g., World Bank Enterprise Surveys) tracking employment and revenue changes in import-competing SMEs before and after trade liberalization episodes, matched with credit access indicators. — Directly tests whether SMEs with limited credit access experience more persistent income losses compared to larger firms or credit-unconstrained SMEs, controlling for sector and time.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of trade adjustment with heterogeneous firms and credit constraints (e.g., Melitz-type models extended with financial frictions), simulating income loss persistence under different SME dominance scenarios. — Provides a causal mechanism linking credit constraints to slower recovery and deeper income losses, which can be calibrated to developing economy parameters for refutability.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing empirical studies on trade liberalization and labor market adjustment, focusing on heterogeneity by firm size and credit access in developing countries (e.g., reviews by Goldberg & Pavcnik, or Harrison & McMillan). — Synthesizes available evidence to assess whether the hypothesized pattern holds across contexts, identifying gaps and potential confounders.

qualifier.temporal: during the first 3-5 years after trade liberalization
qualifier.geographic: in developing economies with large import-competing sectors dominated by SMEs

C006.subject: Free trade policies
C006.object: immediate net employment gains and income increases in import-competing sectors of developing economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade policies immediate net employment gains and income increases in import-competing sectors of developing economies]

[PATH:empirical] Country-level labor force surveys and household income panels (e.g., LSMS, ENEMDU) from developing economies that underwent trade liberalization (e.g., India 1991, Mexico 1994, Vietnam 2000s), analyzing employment and income changes in import-competing sectors (e.g., textiles, agriculture) during the first 3-5 years post-reform. — Directly tests the hypothesis by measuring actual net employment and income changes in the specified sectors and time frame, providing causal evidence via difference-in-differences or fixed-effects models.

[PATH:theoretical] Simulation studies using computable general equilibrium (CGE) models calibrated to developing economies with large import-competing sectors, incorporating short-run labor market rigidities (e.g., minimum wages, sectoral mobility constraints). — Allows controlled exploration of mechanisms (e.g., firm exit, reallocation frictions) that could produce net employment losses or gains, clarifying conditions under which the hypothesis holds or fails.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing empirical literature on trade liberalization and labor outcomes in developing economies, focusing on studies that report short-term (1-5 year) effects on import-competing sectors. — Synthesizes evidence from multiple contexts to assess overall support for the hypothesis, identifying common patterns, effect sizes, and sources of heterogeneity (e.g., by region or policy design).

qualifier.temporal: during the first 3-5 years after trade liberalization
qualifier.geographic: in developing economies with large import-competing sectors

C007.subject: Free trade policies
C007.object: net welfare effects that are simultaneously beneficial and harmful to developing economies only when institutional capacity to redistribute gains is weak, and specifically this dual effect becomes unambiguously positive when institutional capacity to redistribute gains is strong
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade policies net welfare effects that are simultaneously beneficial and harmful to developing economies only when institutional capacity to redistribute gains is weak, and specifically this dual effect becomes unambiguously positive when institutional capacity to redistribute gains is strong]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of trade liberalization episodes in developing countries with varying levels of institutional capacity (e.g., Vietnam vs. Sub-Saharan African nations), measuring changes in income inequality and poverty alongside institutional strength indices (e.g., World Governance Indicators). — Directly tests the condition that strong institutional capacity turns net welfare effects positive, by contrasting outcomes across institutional contexts.

[PATH:theoretical] Rodrik, D. (2011). The Globalization Paradox: Democracy and the Future of the World Economy. New York: W.W. Norton. — Provides foundational theory on how domestic institutions mediate the distributional effects of trade, offering mechanisms for why strong redistribution capacity can resolve the dual-effect into unambiguous gains.

C008.subject: Free trade policies
C008.object: net welfare effects that are unambiguously positive for developing economies regardless of institutional capacity to redistribute gains
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Free trade policies net welfare effects that are unambiguously positive for developing economies regardless of institutional capacity to redistribute gains]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative panel studies on trade liberalization and income inequality in East Asia vs. Latin America (e.g., using World Bank or UNU-WIDER data) — Directly tests whether institutional capacity to redistribute gains mediates net welfare effects; East Asia often has stronger institutions, Latin America weaker, so contrasting outcomes can refute or support the 'regardless' claim.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of ex-post evaluations of free trade agreements' impact on poverty and growth in developing economies (e.g., from NBER or CEPR working papers) — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether positive net welfare effects are truly unambiguous or conditional on institutional factors like social safety nets or governance quality.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of trade with heterogeneous agents and institutional frictions (e.g., extensions of the Melitz or Helpman models incorporating redistribution mechanisms) — Provides formal predictions about conditions under which trade gains can be unambiguously positive without redistribution; can identify institutional thresholds that would falsify the hypothesis.

qualifier.geographic: developing economies in East Asia and Latin America
